introduction_markdown:
**Duration: three hours.** Enter the information required in the boxes of the flap. Answer ALL the SIX questions in this booklet. The mark allocation is indicated for each question. Each question carries 20 marks. Verify that this booklet contains six questions, no questions are repeated and there are no blank pages. Inform the invigilator in case this booklet contains less than six questions, questions are repeated or there are blank pages so that the booklet should be changed. Blank spaces in this question booklet may be used for rough work. In calculations you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. All necessary working must be shown. No marks will be awarded for answers without brief statements showing how the answers have been obtained. Noiseless calculators may be used.

**Useful data:** $R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$ or $0.082\ \mathrm{atm\,dm^{3}\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$. One atmosphere (1 atm) = 1 Pa = $1.01\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$ (as printed). Relative atomic masses (RAM): C = 12.0, O = 16.0, S = 32.0, H = 1.0, Cl = 35.5.

The paper has three sections: Section A - Physical and General Chemistry (questions 1 and 2); Section B - Inorganic Chemistry (questions 3 and 4); Section C - Organic Chemistry (questions 5 and 6). All six questions are compulsory.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The elements in period 2 of the periodic table are Li-Ne.

(i) Complete the table below by giving the structure of each element.

| Element | Li | Be | B | C | N | O | F | Ne |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Structure | | | | | | | | |

(ii) How does the boiling point of the elements vary across this period?

(iii) The ions of Li, Be and B are said to be isoelectronic. What are isoelectronic ions?

(iv) State and explain the trend in atomic radius across the period.

Trend:

Explanation: *[7 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Structures of the period 2 elements.**

| Element | Li | Be | B | C | N | O | F | Ne |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Structure | giant metallic | giant metallic | giant covalent (macromolecular) | giant covalent (diamond or graphite) | simple molecular, diatomic $\mathrm{N_2}$ | simple molecular, diatomic $\mathrm{O_2}$ | simple molecular, diatomic $\mathrm{F_2}$ | monatomic (single atoms, simple molecular) |

**(ii) Variation of boiling point.** The boiling point **rises from lithium to a maximum at the giant covalent elements boron and carbon** (very high, above about $3500^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; lithium about $1340^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and beryllium about $2470^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ because the metallic bonding gets stronger with more delocalised electrons and a smaller, more highly charged ion), then **falls sharply** to very low values for the simple molecular elements nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine and neon (all below $-180^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; neon the lowest, about $-246^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$). Melting or boiling these only overcomes weak **van der Waals (London dispersion) forces** between molecules or atoms, not strong covalent or metallic bonds.

**(iii) Isoelectronic ions** are ions (or atoms) that have the **same number of electrons, and hence the same electronic configuration**. Here $\mathrm{Li^+}$, $\mathrm{Be^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{B^{3+}}$ each have 2 electrons ($1s^2$) although they have different numbers of protons (3, 4 and 5).

**(iv) Atomic radius.**

**Trend:** the atomic radius **decreases** from lithium to neon (across the period from left to right).

**Explanation:** the **nuclear charge increases by one proton** from one element to the next, while the extra electrons are added to the **same outer shell** ($n = 2$), so the **shielding by inner electrons stays about the same**. The **effective nuclear charge increases**, pulling the outer electrons closer to the nucleus and decreasing the radius.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Give one characteristic property of transition metals

(ii) State and explain the trend in first ionization energy across the first transition series. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) A characteristic property of transition metals** (any one): they show **variable oxidation states** (for example $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$, $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$ to $\mathrm{Mn^{7+}}$); they form **coloured compounds and ions**; they form **complex ions**; they act as **catalysts**; they are paramagnetic when they have unpaired d electrons.

**(ii) First ionisation energy across the first transition series ($\mathrm{Sc}$ to $\mathrm{Zn}$).**

**Trend:** the first ionisation energy **increases only slightly** across the series (from about $630\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ for Sc to about $900\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ for Zn, with small irregularities), a much smaller increase than across a main-group period.

**Explanation:** the nuclear charge increases by one at each step, but the extra electrons enter the **inner $3d$ subshell**, not the outer $4s$ subshell from which the electron is removed. The $3d$ electrons **shield the $4s$ electrons** from the increasing nuclear charge, so the **effective nuclear charge rises only slightly** and the ionisation energy changes little.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The complex, $[\mathrm{CoCl_2(en)_2}]^{+}$ contains a polydentate ligand.

(i) Name the complex.

(ii) What is a polydentate ligand?

(iii) Name one type of isomerism exhibited by the complex and give the structures of the isomers. *[5 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Name.** $\mathrm{en}$ is ethane-1,2-diamine ($\mathrm{H_2NCH_2CH_2NH_2}$), a neutral ligand. Oxidation state of cobalt: $x + 2(-1) + 2(0) = +1$, so $x = +3$.

**Dichlorobis(ethane-1,2-diamine)cobalt(III) ion** (ligands in alphabetical order: chlorido, then ethane-1,2-diamine).

**(ii) Polydentate ligand.** A **polydentate ligand** is a ligand that has **two or more donor atoms**, each with a lone pair, so that it forms **two or more coordinate (dative) bonds to the same central metal ion**. Ethane-1,2-diamine is **bidentate** (two nitrogen donor atoms) and forms a five-membered chelate ring; $\mathrm{EDTA^{4-}}$ is hexadentate.

**(iii) Isomerism: geometric (cis-trans) isomerism.** The complex is **octahedral** with cobalt at the centre; each en occupies two adjacent positions.

- **trans-isomer:** the two $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ ligands are **opposite each other** ($180^{\circ}$, on the vertical axis); the two en ligands lie in the horizontal plane around cobalt. It has a plane of symmetry and is not chiral. It is the green isomer.
- **cis-isomer:** the two $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ ligands are **next to each other** ($90^{\circ}$); the two en ligands are arranged so that each en spans two adjacent positions. It is violet.

The cis form has no plane of symmetry and exists as a **pair of non-superimposable mirror images (optical isomers)**; so the complex also shows optical isomerism (cis form only).

questions.enonce_markdown: Nitric acid is manufactured industrially by catalytic oxidation of ammonia. Give balanced equations for the reactions involved in the manufacture. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
This is the **Ostwald process**.

1. Catalytic oxidation of ammonia (platinum-rhodium gauze catalyst, about $900^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$):
 $4\mathrm{NH_3(g)} + 5\mathrm{O_2(g)} \rightarrow 4\mathrm{NO(g)} + 6\mathrm{H_2O(g)}$
2. The nitrogen monoxide is oxidised by more air on cooling:
 $2\mathrm{NO(g)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NO_2(g)}$
3. The nitrogen dioxide is absorbed in water in the presence of excess oxygen:
 $4\mathrm{NO_2(g)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightarrow 4\mathrm{HNO_3(aq)}$
 (or $3\mathrm{NO_2} + \mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{HNO_3} + \mathrm{NO}$, the $\mathrm{NO}$ being recycled).

Atom check for equation 1: N 4 = 4; H 12 = 12; O 10 = 4 + 6. Equation 3: N 4 = 4; H 4 = 4; O $8 + 2 + 2 = 12 = 12$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
One environmental hazard in the manufacture of sulphuric acid is "acid rain".

(i) What is acid rain?

(ii) Give one effect of "acid rain" on the environment. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Acid rain** is **rain with a pH lower than about 5.6** (the pH of unpolluted rain, which contains dissolved carbon dioxide). It is formed when the acidic gases **sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides** released into the atmosphere dissolve in rainwater and are oxidised to **sulphuric acid and nitric acid**: $\mathrm{SO_2} + \tfrac12\mathrm{O_2} + \mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow \mathrm{H_2SO_4}$.

**(ii) One effect** (any one): it **acidifies lakes and rivers and kills fish and other aquatic life**; it **damages trees and vegetation** and leaches nutrients from soil; it **corrodes buildings and statues made of limestone or marble and metal structures** ($\mathrm{CaCO_3} + \mathrm{H_2SO_4} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaSO_4} + \mathrm{CO_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}$).
